text: KILLing the blocking session would end the immediate freeze, but it's not a fix. It's a workaround that would recur every single morning, and killing a session mid-transaction can leave appointment data in an inconsistent, partially-applied state. The real fix addresses why the transaction stays open so long in the first place.

Lesson 8 found the cause precisely: the batch job updates appointment statuses, then waits to commit until a separate, slower step — sending confirmation messages — finishes for every row. Sending a message has nothing to do with the database transaction itself.

The fix is to commit first and send messages after. Only the actual data change happens inside the transaction boundary — a fast, purely database-side operation — so locks are held for a fraction of a second instead of however long message-sending takes.

Re-run the batch job and the blocking-chain query from Lesson 8 side by side, during a simulated busy window. Before the fix, several blocked scheduling sessions for minutes at a time. After the fix, empty, or blocking lasting milliseconds — the normal, healthy kind that resolves on its own.

This generalizes well beyond this one fix. A slow, non-database step — messaging, file I-O, an external API call — ending up inside a transaction boundary out of convenience rather than necessity is the single most common real cause of blocking in production systems. Next lesson: keeping Billing's index fix from quietly degrading over time.
